text: A dbt model that runs without erroring isn't the same as a model that's correct. This lesson adds real tests to Driftwood's project -- the kind that would have actually caught a specific, realistic mistake -- and documents it so someone other than its author can understand it.

Each generic test maps to a real risk. not_null on subscriber_id catches a malformed billing row that would silently break the join in int_subscriber_activity. accepted_values on event_type catches a typo'd or new event type the pipeline wasn't built to expect. unique on dim_subscribers' subscriber_id catches the single most damaging failure for a dimension table feeding a dashboard: duplicate subscriber rows silently inflating the subscriber count.
dbt's own Test Status lens shows exactly this at a glance across a real project -- every model carrying a pass, fail, or warn badge for its latest test run.

A singular test is just a SQL query -- dbt considers it failed if that query returns any rows. This one encodes a fact no generic test could: a subscriber's cancellation can never happen before their first-seen date. If the pipeline ever produces a row where it does, that's a real upstream problem worth stopping on.

Documenting fct_subscriptions' grain -- one row per event, not per subscriber -- is exactly the kind of thing a new analyst would otherwise have to ask someone, guess wrong, and silently miscount subscribers against.
Running dbt docs generate turns every model, column description, test, and the full ref() dependency graph into a browsable, searchable site -- exactly this real dbt Catalog view.
Next lesson: orchestrating all of this with Airflow, so it runs automatically every day instead of by hand.
